data.claim: W.merge returning a timed_out failure after the commit landed makes merge() record failed and refuse; judging by whether base contains the branch fixes it
data.falsifier: regression test passes on unfixed code
data.probe_output: AssertionError exit=1 reason='git merge timed out after 300s'
data.question: Does a git killed at timeout after committing leave merge reporting refused?

evidence.note: research note filed; probe failed on unfixed code with exit 1 'git merge timed out after 300s'
ddflow brief --item fix-B04bab3d1b3 read; decisions D-rules-* irrelevant to merge internals
commit on ddflow/fix-B04bab3d1b3: _landed_anyway in ddflow/api/lifecycle/merge.py, test tests/test_merge_timeout_landed.py

chunk_findings.detail:
The landed check tests the *branch ref* (`wt.branch`), while the run's actual source head is `branch_head`, which for a non-borrowed worktree is taken from the worktree itself (`branch_head = W.head_sha(wt.path)`), not from the ref — the `borrowed` split two lines above exists precisely because these two are not the same source for every caller (and `branch_head` is what the code records as evidence for what was merged). So the code can conclude "landed" from a commit that is not the one this run tried to land.

Concrete input: a non-borrowed item worktree whose HEAD (`branch_head = H`) is ahead of its branch ref, with `wt.branch` pointing at O, an ancestor of `main` (e.g. the worktree carries the item's new commits while the local ref still points at the branch point; ddflow's non-borrowed path deliberately reads the head from `wt.path`, not from `W.rev(repo, wt.branch)`). Run `merge`: `_lands_nothing` sees H has commits `main` lacks, so no refusal; `landed_before = O0`; the `git merge` attempt fails (conflict, or the timeout this change is about) without committing H. Meanwhile another merge advances `main` to M (which contains O because O was already reachable, but not H). `_landed_anyway` then sees `now = M != landed_before = O0` and `W.is_merged(repo, wt.branch = O, wt.base = main) == True`, returns the note, and the item is recorded as `"passed"` with `reason`/`note` asserting "git … after the merge commit landed on main"; `_dispose_tree` then deletes the worktree/branch. H is nowhere on base — the merge gate is reported passed for a merge that never landed, and the item's commits are discarded. Using `branch_head` (or requiring `now` to contain `branch_head`) would test the commit the run was actually merging, consistent with the evidence field written two lines above.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/merge.py:253 (`_landed_anyway` -> `W.is_merged(repo, wt.branch, wt.base)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test performs the real merge first (`real(*a, **kw)`) and only then fabricates a timed-out `GitResult`. Base therefore holds the branch no matter what the code under test does, and the test's success hinges entirely on the implementation returning `OK` for that fabricated result. A regression that maps "merge timed out" → success unconditionally (never consulting containment) passes this test identically: kill `git merge` at 300 s with the commit not yet created (e.g. `git` hung before writing the merge commit, or a conflicted merge where `MERGE_HEAD` exists and base does not contain the branch) and the same code path would report the gate passed with the same "timed out" note. So the change ships its detection heuristic with only the trivial-positive case covered; the negative input the heuristic exists to reject (timeout, branch *not* contained in base → must stay failed/refused) has no test. That is the input that makes the reviewed behaviour wrong, and the suite cannot see it.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_merge_timeout_landed.py:24-45 (landed_then_killed / test body)

chunk_findings.detail: `assert '"failed"' not in shown` does not verify the merge gate was recorded as passed; it only verifies that the literal substring `"failed"` is absent from the `gate status` output. If the new code never recorded the merge gate at all (e.g. `gate status T1` renders an empty object, or the merge gate key is missing), the assertion passes vacuously while the gate machinery has silently produced nothing. The same substring check is also fragile in the other direction: any unrelated occurrence of the token (e.g. a boolean field rendered as `"failed": false`) makes the test fail on correct code. Asserting the parsed gate's status field is `passed` (and that the entry exists) is what the intent promises, and is not what this line checks.
